extraction_notes.note: The informal proof of Proposition 1 ends with \qedsymbol and no period, so the finishing step flags it as ending mid-sentence; the span is the author's full argument.

Label eq:tanh1 is defined twice (for v ~ 1/sqrt(N) and for the tanh pdf); the figure caption's \ref to it means the pdf (EP16). Also \enum{seq1} sits outside its equation, so eq:seq1 attaches to a section heading.
The text says the 30-layer network converges and the 22-layer one does not, which reverses the earlier description; the statement is copied as written.
Definition or claim: the sentence asserts equal moments by symmetry, but its main role is introducing $\mu_m$ and $s_m^2$.
The main results (general initialization formula, re-derived He initialization) are numbered equations that the text never names as results, so they stay equation nodes.
Single sentences introduce several symbols at once; a sentence can't be split, so each is one definition node with all symbols in definiendum.

Most of the argument is a chain of prose derivations linking numbered equations, with no proof environments. The equation-to-equation dependencies were added as uses edges by hand, and the connecting prose gets no node.
The CIFAR-10 experimental protocol (architecture, 10 training iterations, top-5 accuracy) is not an algorithm node; only its reported outcome is kept as a numerical claim.

nodes.name: Xavier optimal variance for linear activations
nodes.statement: The first systematic analysis of this problem was conducted by Glorot and Bengio \cite{glorot2010understanding} who showed that for a linear activation function, the optimal value of $v^{2} = 1/N$, where $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer.
nodes.statement_short: For a linear activation, the optimal weight variance is $v^2=1/N$ with $N$ the fan-in.
conclusions: the optimal value of $v^{2} = 1/N$, where $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer

nodes.name: Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: Although the paper makes several assumptions about the inputs to the model, it works extremely well in many cases and is widely used in the initialization of neural networks to date; this initialization scheme is commonly referred to as the {\it{Xavier initialization}}.
nodes.statement_short: The $v^2=1/N$ scheme of Glorot and Bengio is called the Xavier initialization.

nodes.name: He initialization
nodes.statement: In an important follow up paper, He and colleagues \cite{he2015delving} argue that the {\it{Xavier initialization}} does not work well with the RELU activation function, and instead propose an initialization of $v^{2} = 2/N$ (commonly referred to as the {\it{He initialization}}).
nodes.statement_short: He et al. propose $v^2=2/N$ for RELU, called the He initialization.

nodes.name: Why the 30-layer RELU network converges with He but not Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: In support of their initialization, they provide an example of a 30 layer neural network which converges with the {\it{He initialization}}, but not under the {\it{Xavier initialization}}. To the best of my knowledge, the precise reason for the convergence of one method and the non-convergence of the other is not fully understood.
nodes.statement_short: Explain why a deep RELU network converges under He but not under Xavier initialization.

nodes.name: Deep neural network with $M$ layers
nodes.statement: Consider a deep neural network with $M$ layers.

nodes.name: Pre-activation recursion
nodes.statement: y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij} \enum{in1}
nodes.statement_short: Pre-activation $y_m(i)$ is the weighted sum of layer inputs.
nodes.label: eq:in1

nodes.name: Activation recursion
nodes.statement: x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{g}(y_{m}(i)). \enum{in2}
nodes.label: eq:in2

nodes.name: Network notation $p_{ij}$, ${\bf{W}}_{m}$, $g$, $N$
nodes.statement: Here $p_{j} = {\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)$, ${\bf{W}}_{m}$ is a matrix of weights for the $m^{th}$ layer, $g$ is the non-linear activation function, and $N$ is the number of nodes in the hidden layers respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Names the summands $p_{ij}$, weight matrix $W_m$, activation $g$ and width $N$.

nodes.name: I.i.d. normal weights
nodes.statement: The weights ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ are assumed to be independent identically distributed normal random variables with mean 0 and variance $v^{2}$.

nodes.name: I.i.d. standardized inputs
nodes.statement: Consistent with the assumptions in \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving}, I assume that the inputs to the first layer are independent and identically distributed random variables with mean 0 and variance 1.

nodes.name: $r_m$ and $u_m^2$
nodes.statement: For convenience, I use $r_{m}$ and $u_{m}^{2}$ to denote the mean and variance of $y_{m}(i)$ respectively.

nodes.name: $\mu_m$ and $s_m^2$
nodes.statement: Due to the symmetry in the problem, all inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer will have the same means and variances during the first forward pass (i.e., $E(x_{m}(i)) = \mu_m$ and $Var(x_{m}(i)) = s_{m}^{2}$ for all $i$); the covariances between the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer need not be 0.
nodes.statement_short: By symmetry all inputs to layer $m$ share mean $\mu_m$ and variance $s_m^2$ in the first forward pass.

nodes.name: Variance-preserving weight initialization
nodes.statement: The goal is to find the value of $v^{2}$ which ensures that $s_{1}^{2} \approx s_{2}^{2} ...\approx s_{M}^{2} = 1$ during the first forward pass.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $v^2$ so the layer-input variances stay equal to 1 across layers.

nodes.name: Independence of weights and layer inputs
nodes.statement: During the first iteration, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$
conclusions: $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in (\ref {eq:in1}) and (\ref {eq:in2}), $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer. Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$. Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$\qedsymbol
nodes.statement_short: Direct: $x_m$ is a function of earlier weights and inputs only, which are independent of $W_m$.

nodes.name: Express inputs via earlier layers
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in (\ref {eq:in1}) and (\ref {eq:in2}), $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer.
nodes.statement_short: Write $x_m(k)$ as a function of earlier weights and first-layer inputs.

nodes.name: Independence of functions
nodes.statement: Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Independence passes to functions of independent quantities; conclude.

nodes.name: Independence of products
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$\qedsymbol
nodes.statement_short: Extend independence to products $x_m(k)x_m(l)$.

nodes.name: Pre-activation mean is zero
nodes.statement: r_{m} = E(y_{m}(i)) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E(x_{m}(j)) = 0. \enum{in201}
nodes.label: eq:in201

nodes.name: Second moment expansion of $y_m(i)$
nodes.statement: \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= E\left(\sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right)^{2} \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) + 2\sum E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right). \\ \enum{in203} \end{split}
nodes.label: eq:in203

nodes.name: Pre-activation variance $u_m^2 = Nv^2(s_m^2+\mu_m^2)$
nodes.statement: \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= Nv^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ \enum{in204} \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: Pre-activation variance equals $Nv^2$ times the second moment of the layer inputs.
nodes.label: eq:in204

nodes.name: Variance formula holds for any input covariance
nodes.statement: Interestingly, this result holds for any arbitrary covariance structure of the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer.

nodes.name: Large width
nodes.statement: To answer this question, I make the additional assumption that the number of nodes in the hidden layer ($N$) is `large'; this assumption is reasonable given that most neural networks have several hundred nodes in the hidden layers.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the hidden-layer width $N$ is large.

nodes.name: Approximate normality of pre-activations
nodes.statement: $y_{m}(i)$ will be approximately normally distributed for all values of $m$ and $i$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right) = 0$. Furthermore, for $j \neq k$, \begin{equation} \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split} \end{equation} where the last equality follows from (\ref {eq:in2041}). This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables. Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}. Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}). Thus, $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to to be approximately normally distributed during most iterations. \qedsymbol
nodes.statement_short: Show the summands $p_{ij}$ are mean zero and uncorrelated, then invoke the Central Limit Theorem for large $N$.

nodes.name: Summands uncorrelated
nodes.statement: \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split}

nodes.name: Summands are centered and uncorrelated
nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right) = 0$. Furthermore, for $j \neq k$, \begin{equation} \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split} \end{equation} where the last equality follows from (\ref {eq:in2041}).
nodes.statement_short: Show $E(p_{ij})=0$ and $Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})=0$.

nodes.name: Apply Central Limit Theorem
nodes.statement: This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables. Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}.
nodes.statement_short: Treat summands as i.i.d. and apply the CLT for large $N$.

nodes.name: Dependent case and conclusion
nodes.statement: Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}). Thus, $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to to be approximately normally distributed during most iterations. \qedsymbol
nodes.statement_short: CLT conditions are weak even under dependence; conclude approximate normality.

nodes.name: Layer-input mean $\approx g(0)$
nodes.statement: \mu_{m+1} = E(x_{m+1}(i)) \approx g(0). \enum{in206}
nodes.label: eq:in206

nodes.name: All layer means equal $g(0)$
nodes.statement: \mu_{j} = g(0) \mbox{ for all } j\geq 1 \enum{in2061}.
nodes.label: eq:in2061

nodes.name: Variance recursion for differentiable activations
nodes.statement_short: Next-layer variance $\approx N g'(0)^2 v^2 (s_m^2+g(0)^2)$.
nodes.label: eq:in207

nodes.name: General weight initialization for activations differentiable at 0
nodes.statement_short: Variance-preserving weight variance $v^2 = 1/(N g'(0)^2 (1+g(0)^2))$ for any activation differentiable at 0.
nodes.label: eq:in208

nodes.name: Backward-pass constraint unnecessary
nodes.statement: In their calculations, \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving} impose an additional set of constraints to ensure that the variance is maintained even during the backward pass. I believe that this is not required, since the requirement that the variance of the inputs at each layer be the same ensures that the gradient flows through in the backward pass.
nodes.statement_short: Forward variance preservation suffices; the backward-pass constraints of Glorot-Bengio and He are not needed.

nodes.name: Hyperbolic tangent activation
nodes.statement: g(x) =\mbox{tanh}(x),

nodes.name: Weight scale for tanh
nodes.statement: v \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{tanh1}
nodes.statement_short: For tanh, $v\approx 1/\sqrt{N}$, the Xavier initialization.
nodes.label: eq:tanh1

nodes.name: Sequential saturation under tanh
nodes.statement: In their analysis of a neural network with the hyperbolic tangent activations, \cite{glorot2010understanding} find that the deeper layers in the neural network have a greater proportion of unsaturated nodes than the shallower layers. As is stated in their paper, `why this is happening remains to be understood'.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Why do deeper tanh layers have more unsaturated nodes than shallower ones?

nodes.name: Explanation of sequential saturation
nodes.statement: To explain their finding, I begin by noting that in \cite{glorot2010understanding}, the authors initialize the weights using samples from a uniform distribution $\left(U[-1/\sqrt{N},1/\sqrt{N}]\right)$ having a variance of $1/3N$. Therefore, from (\ref {eq:in2061}) and (\ref {eq:in207}), with $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$, we have $\mu_{m} = 0$ and \begin{equation} s_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{3}s_{m}^{2} < s_{m}^{2} \end{equation} \enum{seq1} respectively. From (\ref {eq:in204}), this implies that $u_{m+1}^{2}<u_{m}^{2}$ for all $m$ (i.e., $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$). Furthermore from proposition 2, $y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. Therefore, $x_{m+1}(i)$ will be the tanh transformation of a normal random variable. Using results from \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{tanh}(y_{m}(i))$ will have a probability density function (pdf) given by \begin{equation} f(y) = \frac{1}{1-y^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi u_{m}^{2}}}\mbox{e}^{\left({-\frac{t_{y}^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}\right)} \enum{tanh1}, \end{equation} where \begin{equation} t_{y} = \frac{1}{2} ln\left(\frac{1+y}{1-y}\right). \end{equation} Plots of this pdf for different values of $u_{m}$ (provided in Figure \ref{fig:tanh}) produce trends similar to those observed by the simulation studies of \cite{glorot2010understanding} (figure 4 in their paper). A comparison of Figure \ref{fig:tanh} and figure 4 of \cite{glorot2010understanding} suggests that $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, as is expected. From the results in \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, we expect the activations to be (a) approximately normally distributed when $u_{m}$ is close to 0 and (b) bimodally distributed with local maximas near -1 and +1 when $u_{m}$ is close to 1.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Uniform init with variance $1/3N$ shrinks $u_m^2$ geometrically; the tanh-of-normal density then shows less saturation for small $u_m$.

nodes.name: Variance shrinkage under Glorot uniform initialization
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Density of tanh of a normal variable
nodes.statement: f(y) = \frac{1}{1-y^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi u_{m}^{2}}}\mbox{e}^{\left({-\frac{t_{y}^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}\right)} \enum{tanh1},
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Pdf of $\tanh$ of a $N(0,u_m^2)$ variable.
nodes.label: eq:tanh1

nodes.name: Inverse tanh substitution
nodes.statement: t_{y} = \frac{1}{2} ln\left(\frac{1+y}{1-y}\right).
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent

nodes.name: Variance shrinks by factor 1/3
nodes.statement: To explain their finding, I begin by noting that in \cite{glorot2010understanding}, the authors initialize the weights using samples from a uniform distribution $\left(U[-1/\sqrt{N},1/\sqrt{N}]\right)$ having a variance of $1/3N$. Therefore, from (\ref {eq:in2061}) and (\ref {eq:in207}), with $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$, we have $\mu_{m} = 0$ and \begin{equation} s_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{3}s_{m}^{2} < s_{m}^{2} \end{equation} \enum{seq1} respectively.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Glorot's uniform initialization has variance $1/3N$, so $s_{m+1}^2 = s_m^2/3$.

nodes.name: Pre-activation variance decreases
nodes.statement: From (\ref {eq:in204}), this implies that $u_{m+1}^{2}<u_{m}^{2}$ for all $m$ (i.e., $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$).
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Hence $u_m^2$ decreases with depth.

nodes.name: Activation density
nodes.statement: Furthermore from proposition 2, $y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. Therefore, $x_{m+1}(i)$ will be the tanh transformation of a normal random variable. Using results from \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{tanh}(y_{m}(i))$ will have a probability density function (pdf) given by \begin{equation} f(y) = \frac{1}{1-y^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi u_{m}^{2}}}\mbox{e}^{\left({-\frac{t_{y}^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}\right)} \enum{tanh1}, \end{equation} where \begin{equation} t_{y} = \frac{1}{2} ln\left(\frac{1+y}{1-y}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Pre-activations are normal, so activations follow the tanh-of-normal density.

nodes.name: Comparison with simulations
nodes.statement: Plots of this pdf for different values of $u_{m}$ (provided in Figure \ref{fig:tanh}) produce trends similar to those observed by the simulation studies of \cite{glorot2010understanding} (figure 4 in their paper). A comparison of Figure \ref{fig:tanh} and figure 4 of \cite{glorot2010understanding} suggests that $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, as is expected.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Plotted densities match Glorot-Bengio simulations.

nodes.name: Shape of density versus $u_m$
nodes.statement: From the results in \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, we expect the activations to be (a) approximately normally distributed when $u_{m}$ is close to 0 and (b) bimodally distributed with local maximas near -1 and +1 when $u_{m}$ is close to 1.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Density is near-normal for small $u_m$ and bimodal near $\pm1$ for $u_m$ near 1.

nodes.name: Saturation decreases with depth under tanh
nodes.statement: Accordingly, since $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, we expect the activations from the shallower layers to be more saturated (i.e., more concentrated near -1 and +1), and the saturation in the activations to reduce as we go to the deeper layers in the network.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
assumptions: since $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$
conclusions: we expect the activations from the shallower layers to be more saturated (i.e., more concentrated near -1 and +1), and the saturation in the activations to reduce as we go to the deeper layers in the network

nodes.name: Sigmoid activation
nodes.statement: g(x) = \frac{1}{1 + \mbox{e}^{-x}}

nodes.name: Weight scale for sigmoid
nodes.statement: v \approx \frac{3.6}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{relur}
nodes.statement_short: For the sigmoid, $v\approx 3.6/\sqrt{N}$.
nodes.label: eq:relur

nodes.name: Sigmoid initialization outperforms Xavier on CIFAR-10
nodes.statement: A comparison of the validation accuracies for the 2 cases is provided in Figure \ref{fig:conv}, which shows that the convergence appears to stall with the {\it{Xavier initialization}}, but proceeds rapidly with the initialization proposed in (\ref {eq:relur}).
nodes.statement_short: On a 10-layer CIFAR-10 sigmoid network, training stalls with Xavier but converges with $v\approx3.6/\sqrt N$.

nodes.name: Rectified Linear Unit (RELU)
nodes.statement: We are interested in in the mean and variance of $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{max}(0,y_{m}(i))$.

nodes.name: Mean of RELU output
nodes.statement: \mu_{m+1} = E(y_{m}(i){\bf{I}}(y_{m}(i)>0)) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{e}^{-t}dt = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. \enum{relu1}
nodes.statement_short: $\mu_{m+1}=u_m/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for RELU.
nodes.label: eq:relu1

nodes.name: Second moment of RELU output
nodes.statement: E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{1}{{u\sqrt{2\pi}}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2}. \enum{relu2}
nodes.label: eq:relu2

nodes.name: Variance of RELU output
nodes.statement_short: $s_{m+1}^2\approx 0.34 u_m^2$ for RELU.
nodes.label: eq:relu3

nodes.name: Required pre-activation variance for RELU
nodes.statement: u_{m}^{2} \approx 3. \enum{relu301}
nodes.label: eq:relu301

nodes.name: Exponential variance decay with depth
nodes.statement: Equation (\ref {eq:relu602}) shows that the variance of the inputs to the deeper layers is exponentially smaller than the variance of the inputs to the shallower layer.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.
nodes.statement_short: Under Xavier with RELU, deeper-layer input variance is exponentially smaller.

nodes.name: Xavier worsens with depth for RELU
nodes.statement: Therefore, the deeper the neural network, the worse the performance of the {\it{Xavier Initialization}} will be.

nodes.name: Explanation of 22- vs 30-layer convergence
nodes.statement: From (\ref {eq:relu602}), $s_{22}^{2} \approx 1.62 \times 10^{-7}$ and $s_{30}^{2} \approx 6.33 \times 10^{-10}$. Thus the variance in the input to the $30^{th}$ layer will be $(0.51)^{8} = 3 \times 10^{-3}$ times smaller than the variance to the $22^{nd}$ layer, and explains the possible reason why the 30 layer neural network described in \cite{he2015delving} converges, but the 22 layer neural network does not.
nodes.section: To converge or not to converge, that is the question.
nodes.statement_short: Layer-30 input variance is $0.51^8\approx3\times10^{-3}$ times layer 22's, explaining the convergence gap.
